1:
Gill dates the assembly from Jarchi, the day after the descent from the mount, Moses being eager to begin the tabernacle, the work having been held up by the golden calf and the making of reconciliation for it. Henry reads the summons of all the congregation as a summons of the heads and rulers, who take their instructions from Moses as he took his from the Lord and pass them on to the people. Moses gave in charge all that God had commanded and no more, so proving faithful to both parties between whom he stood: had he added or diminished he would have been false to each. Yet he was faithful as a servant only, where Christ was faithful as a Son.

The law of rest comes first because it had been pressed on Moses most. Henry takes the six days as days of work for the tabernacle; but on the seventh not a stroke was to be struck, not even at the tabernacle, the sabbath being the elder and the more lasting honour. He offers two further renderings: a sabbath of sabbaths, more excellent than any other feast and destined to outlast them all; and, as some of the Jews would have it, a sabbath and a little sabbath, since they add an hour at each end out of their own time, to show how loth they are to part with it. Wesley states the rule plainly, that the six days' work meant is work for the tabernacle. Gill would render the first clause may be done, every man being free to follow his calling — unless the repetition looks particularly at the tabernacle and orders close work at it.

The prohibition of fire divides them. Gill takes it for a temporary law, not said here as elsewhere to be throughout their generations, and restrained to the season of the building, its purpose being to stop sabbath work on the tabernacle by leaving no fire to heat a tool or melt metal; it can hardly be meant in the strictest sense, since fire is needful in cold weather, and for infants, the aged and the sick. Clarke reports how the Jews themselves limit it, to fire kindled for work or for dressing food, holding it lawful to have light and heat — though they rarely kindle it, getting Christians to do that work for them. Wesley restricts it to servile work, a smith's or a plumber's, and finds no evidence that the prohibition ever reached further. Ellicott approaches it as legislation: the preceding verse mainly repeats an earlier law, but this one is new, or at most implied before — and kindling fire was in those days hard manual labour, got by rubbing two dry sticks together.

On the offering the emphasis falls on the willingness. Clarke identifies it as a terumah, a heave-offering; Gill has every man take part of his own substance according to his ability. Calvin marks a change of grammar, that where the earlier passage used a verb this one uses a noun, willing of heart, though the sense is the same: God asks a cheerful zeal, so that they should give not only abundantly but gladly. A further phrase follows for those whose heart stirred them up, setting them apart from the indifferent and the slow. Henry draws the same lesson from the form of the request: it was no tax but a benevolence, which tells us that God has not made our yoke heavy, being a prince who does not burden his subjects, but draws with the cords of a man; and that he loves a cheerful giver. Since the wise-hearted are called as well as the wealthy, he observes how variously God dispenses his gifts: the rich were to bring materials and the skilful their skill, and the tabernacle had need of both.
7:
Calvin explains why the list is given again at all: having told them to supply the materials, Moses now calls for the industry that will shape and join them, and runs briefly over parts he had described at length before — the epitome being needed to spur them afresh, since instruction is often coldly received without exhortation. Gill takes the wise-hearted for ingenious men skilled in some mechanic art, and his notes identify what each name covers: the tabernacle is not the whole structure but the ten fine linen curtains, the inner ones as Jarchi calls them; the incense altar was overlaid with gold, and so called the golden altar; the pins fastened the curtain-ends into the ground against the wind. On the cloths of service he offers two senses, wrappings for the vessels when the camp moved, or the vestments the priests served in; Clarke guesses at aprons and towels, distinct from the robes of Aaron.

Where a pillaged people found such wealth is asked by two. Calvin answers that they must have been enriched at their departure by the booty God gave them: what Egypt had heaped up by rapacity flowed away by God's secret influence when its people were made prodigal, and as he had blinded them into giving profusely, so he now inclined Israel to spend willingly what they had of his mere grace. Henry adds that since the spoil came by special providence, it was highly fit they should devote part of it to the God they owed it all to.

On the promptness Henry and Calvin divide. Henry admires the speed: they went to their tents at once and did not ask time to consider, lest their zeal cool with delay. Calvin praises the opposite quality in the same act: their departing from Moses' presence shows that they retired to their tents and considered by themselves what to give, so their liberality deserves the greater praise for being premeditated, since a man bountiful on sudden impulse often repents afterwards. On the heart that stirred a man up Calvin adds a caution: the Papists twist the phrase into a proof of free-will, whereas Moses in praising their spontaneity does not exclude the grace of the Spirit, who works within upon the will, so that believers stir up themselves and follow his leading voluntarily. Clarke renders it literally, that the heart was lifted up, the affections set on the work; Wesley finds the motive in love to God, gratitude for what he had done and faith in what he had promised.

That not everyone gave is read out of the same clause. Henry infers from the willing-hearted being singled out that some were not, who loved their gold better than their God and are for the true religion provided it be cheap; Ellicott agrees that some hearts did not stir them, though all classes came and gave to the utmost of their power, so that the people had at last to be restrained. Gill notes that none but the willing were so much as asked. Henry will not have the poor discouraged: those who had no precious stones brought goats' hair and rams' skins, God requiring according to what a man has, two mites from a pauper pleasing him more than talents from a Dives; Calvin makes the same defence of the brass and the shittim-wood. Both dwell on the ornaments — Henry that even the women parted with bracelets and rings, preferring the beautifying of the sanctuary to their own adorning, Calvin that this was no ordinary zeal, since people would sooner suffer cold and hunger than give such things up. What the ornaments were is disputed: Clarke takes the last of the four for a girdle supporting the breasts, while Ellicott says it cannot mean tablets, coming from a root for roundness and standing most likely for a bead necklace of the Egyptian kind.
25:
Three describe the spinners. Gill places them socially, as the common sort, the richer having already been named as bringing jewels of gold. Clarke observes that they had learned the art before and now practised it, God condescending to accept their service, and calls the tool simple — the plain distaff or twirling pin, made of any wood they met with in the wilderness. Ellicott takes wise-hearted to mean only that they had sufficient skill, and notes that the sanctuary's fabrics seem to have used flax and goats' hair alone, the flax being dyed before it was spun; he would render the material not fine linen but white, most Egyptian linen being a yellowish white from flax imperfectly blanched. On the second group he and Gill agree that a harder task is meant, a thread being more difficult to draw from goats' hair than from flax, so only the most skilful undertook it.

The rulers bring what only they had. Gill calls the stones to be set stones of fillings, filling their ouches as a stone fills a ring, and says the spices and oil were of a quality the common people had not; Keil adds that the precious stones and the spices came from the princes, in whose hands such costly things were. Ellicott identifies these rulers with the princes of the tribes: the twelve stones of the breastplate would naturally be given by the chiefs whose names they were to bear, and the ephod's two onyx stones by such as owned stones of that size. Clarke stands back: the men worked and brought offerings, the women spun and brought their ornaments, the rulers delivered up their jewels, and all joined in the service.

Henry reads the naming of the master-workmen as a piece of order: it prevented strife over the office and gave everyone employed someone to take direction from, God being the God of order; and those he called by name he filled with his Spirit, skill even in secular employments being his gift. The work was extraordinary, so the man was qualified extraordinarily — as the apostles, appointed master-builders of the gospel tabernacle, were filled with the Spirit in wisdom and understanding. Wesley repeats it, an extraordinary work requiring an extraordinary qualifying. Calvin makes the appointment an encouragement, the people now seeing that God presided over the work: excellent artificers though the two had been already, they were endowed further, even to a miracle. He thinks the tribe of each is named because so conspicuous a grace deserved remembering in all generations, and that God declares the names glorious in heaven of those who employ the Spirit's gifts in building his spiritual temple. That such talent survived at all in a people so long enslaved he takes for a proof that these endowments were neither natural nor got by industry.

The commission is to work and to teach. Henry notes that they were appointed not only to devise but to work: many are ingenious at cutting out work for other people, but the burdens they bind on others they will not touch with one finger, and fall under the character of slothful servants. Bezaleel had not only power to command but a charge to instruct: those who rule should teach, and those to whom God gives knowledge should not covet to monopolize it. Keil finds the same in the grammar: the putting into the heart to teach qualified him to instruct workmen to prepare the articles under his own eye. Calvin gives the practical reason, that two men could never have finished so arduous a work in their lifetime, and treats the patience it required as itself a gift, since otherwise the fatigue of instructing the ignorant would have defeated them. By wisdom of heart, he adds, understand activity of mind, the heart standing in Scripture not only for the affections but for the understanding.
34:
Gill treats the gift of teaching as a separate endowment from the gift of skill, and the distinction carries his whole reading of these two verses. God had already given Bezaleel wisdom, understanding and knowledge — enough to devise a curious work, to contrive the manner of it, and to know how the thing should actually be performed; what is added here is a capacity for instruction and an inclination of the mind towards it, so that his craft should pass into other hands. The two do not always go together, since not every man of learning has either the aptitude or the appetite to pass it on; and Gill's point is that where they do go together the second is as much of God as the first, put into the heart rather than acquired. What he was to convey, moreover, was precisely the matter he himself had knowledge of: others were to be grounded in the very matters of which he had been given understanding, and drilled in how each piece must be wrought.

He reads the filling with wisdom of heart in the same way. The phrase means wisdom in their heart, and the participle measures it, marking a large rather than an ordinary allowance; whatever discernment a man has, in things natural, civil, moral or spiritual, comes from God and from nowhere else. The trades then named Gill matches to the work each was wanted for. The engraver was needed because stones had to be set in the ephod and in the breastplate. The cunning workman was needed for the curtains of the tabernacle, for the vail that divided the holy place from the holy of holies, and again for the high priest's ephod and breastplate. The embroiderer, working in blue and purple and scarlet and fine linen, had his part both in the various furnishings of the tabernacle and in the dress of those employed about it. The weaver was required in two materials, linen and woollen alike, the one for the curtains and hangings and the other for the garments of the priests. The catalogue then widens to take in whoever laboured at all and whoever devised cunning work, which Gill extends past the crafts already named to any curious workmanship in gold, silver, brass, timber or stone — so that the closing clause gathers in every hand the building could use.
